entities.name: Existing autonomous research systems face severe systemic limitations: there is an ideation-execution gap between computational hypothesis generation and real-w
entities.description: Existing autonomous research systems face severe systemic limitations: there is an ideation-execution gap between computational hypothesis generation and real-world validation, especially when discovery requires interacting with physical environments. Even validated AI discovery systems still need substantial human oversight, and grounding AI in physical and empirical reality remains a central bottleneck for scalable real-world scientific discovery.
entities.evidence_span: Despite these computational advances, existing autonomous research systems face severe systemic limitations.

evidence_spans: Despite these computational advances, existing autonomous research systems face severe systemic limitations.
Empirical evaluations highlight an “ideation-execution” gap
This execution gap presents an additional challenge for real-world, open-ended discovery, which requires interacting with physical environments.

Yet, systems that have produced validated discoveries typically require substantial human oversight, with researchers decomposing problems, verifying intermediate steps, and executing physical experiments.

Closing the gap between what autonomous systems can ideate computationally and what they can validate physically remains the central barrier to scalable, AI-accelerated scientific discovery in the real world.

Despite this progress, grounding AI in both physical and empirical reality remains a critical bottleneck underscoring the ongoing necessity of human-in-the-loop collaboration for real-world validation.
However, transitioning from narrow optimization to open-ended, real-world deployment exposes practical limits.

In an effort to mitigate the possibility of using this system for harm, we integrate a two-layer safety architecture directly into the research workflow
yet this risk has remained largely unaddressed in prior autonomous research systems (Tang et al., 2025b).
prompting broader concerns regarding dual-use safety, epistemic reliability, and the need for rigorous scientific oversight
Addressing this requires compositional safety analysis that evaluates entire research trajectories across multiple steps
deeper methodological issues, such as data leakage, metric misuse, and post-hoc selection bias, require verification mechanisms that go beyond checking outputs against execution logs
Addressing these residual errors will require moving beyond execution logs toward automated semantic code inspection and complete reporting audits.
Autonomous research systems complicate established frameworks for scientific accountability.
Existing regulatory frameworks, including institutional review boards and biosafety committees, were designed for human-led research and do not adequately address autonomous AI systems

The development of robust oversight structures, including auditing standards, reporting protocols, and cross-institutional governance bodies, will be essential as autonomous research systems are deployed at scale

However, CVD growth outcomes are highly sensitive to a large, interdependent parameter space, including furnace geometry, precursor chemistry, gas-flow dynamics, and temperature profiles.
